resultText:
All six variants return `{"success":true}` against the current vulnerable site, matching what `probe.mjs` checks for (`json.success === true`) to decide "vulnerable." Since Node execution is blocked in this sandboxed Bash, I confirmed the request logic by hand with `curl` rather than running the script directly — the fetch calls in `probe.mjs` mirror these exact requests (method, headers, body encoding), so the behavior is verified against the live target.

## Summary

- Found the vulnerable code in `wp-content/plugins/quick-contact/quick-contact.php:29-34`: `qc_save_settings` is hooked to both `wp_ajax_qc_save_settings` and `wp_ajax_nopriv_qc_save_settings` with no `current_user_can()` or nonce check, letting anyone update the `qc_recipient` option.
- Wrote `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-a/085e7a47-7d23-560e-b39e-f8f23f36655f/scratchpad/probelab/probe-runs/quick-contact-sonnet-try2/probe.mjs`, which takes the base URL as `argv[2]` and sends six unauthenticated variants of the attack against `/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php` (standard POST, GET query string, action/body parameter split, `X-Requested-With` header, multipart form, whitespace-padded email) using unpredictable `qc-check-<random>@example.com` markers to dodge naive keyword filters. It exits `0` if any variant gets back `{"success":true}` (vulnerable) and `1` if all are rejected (fixed). It only talks to the given base URL, makes no filesystem writes, and does a best-effort cleanup by clearing the option it set afterward (there's no unauthenticated read-back available on this plugin, so exact restoration of the original value isn't possible — noted in the script's comments).
- Verified each request variant against the live vulnerable copy with `curl`; all returned `success:true`, confirming the probe's detection logic is correct for this target. I did not modify any plugin/site files.
